chapter_theme: The making of wealth: it is the great social force that raises the despised, drives out enemies and brings virtue and pleasure within reach, but only wealth rightly gained deserves pursuit.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its importance (751-753), the way to gain it (754-756), and what it yields (757-760).

751.reading: Apart from wealth, nothing makes persons of no account into persons of account.
751.nuance: பொருள் appears four times, playing on 'wealth' and 'something that counts'. Whether this is approval or a dry observation is left open. Parimelazhagar names the unlearned and low-born and concludes that wealth alone should be amassed, while Kalaignar calls those raised unworthy of regard, which has an edge.

752.reading: Everyone scorns those who have nothing and everyone honours the rich.
752.nuance: The verse states a social fact without saying it is just. Parimelazhagar sharpens it, adding that the poor are scorned though they have every good and the rich honoured though they have every evil, words which aren't in the verse.

753.reading: The unfailing lamp called wealth goes to whatever country one has in mind and cuts away the darkness.
753.nuance: Unlike a lamp, this one travels to where it is intended.

positions.position: The darkness is enmity, and the lamp reaches enemy lands on its owner's behalf.
positions.quote: தன்னைச் செய்தவர்க்கு அவர் நினைத்த தேயத்துச் சென்று பகை என்னும் இருளைக் கெடுக்கும்.

positions.position: The darkness is enmity, and a wealthy king's command runs wherever he intends.
positions.quote: அரசன் பொரு ளுடையனானால், தான் கருதிய தேசமெல்லாம் தன்னாணை நடத்துவானென்றது.

positions.position: The darkness is ordinary suffering, which money in hand drives away anywhere one goes.

754.reading: Wealth that comes with knowledge of the right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure.
754.nuance: The commentators differ on the audience. Parimelazhagar makes 'without wrong' a matter of a king not being tyrannical, while Manakkudavar means no harm to anyone else, and the verse itself names no king.

755.reading: Accumulation of wealth that does not come with grace and love should not be embraced, but let go.
755.nuance: புல்லார் புரள விடல் is more than refusing. It is the gesture of letting something roll away. Coming right after 754 and before 756, it is the chapter's clearest limit.

positions.position: Coming with grace and love means, for a king, taxing no more than the rightful one-sixth.
It applies to any earner: not profiting from others' distress and not losing affection for one's intimates while earning.
positions.quote: பொருள் தேடுங்கால் பிறர் வருத்தத்திற்கு உபகரியாதும், பயின்றார் மாட்டுக் காதலில்லாமலும்

756.reading: Wealth that falls in on its own, wealth from customs, and wealth from crushing his enemies are the king's wealth.
756.nuance: Parimelazhagar takes this as the income beyond the one-sixth of 755. Without that bridge, an income by force would sit oddly next to wealth that comes with grace.

positions.position: உறுபொருள் is ownerless wealth: long-buried treasure and estates without heirs.
positions.quote: வைத்தார் இறந்துபோக நெடுங்காலம் நிலத்தின்கண் கிடந்து பின் கண்டெடுத்தூஉம், தாயத்தார் பெறாததூஉமாம்.

positions.position: உறுபொருள் is revenue connected with protection.

757.reading: The child called grace, born of love, is raised by the wealthy foster-mother called wealth.
757.nuance: This gives a genealogy of compassion. Parimelazhagar distinguishes love, which runs along ties, from grace, which goes to any sufferer. The mother gives birth but cannot rear alone, so wealth is necessary without being the source.

758.reading: Undertaking a task with money in hand is like watching an elephant fight from a hilltop.
758.nuance: The picture's point is the safety of distance. Parimelazhagar says the funded person commissions the able and finishes the work without fear or strain, which is a view of capital as insulation from risk.

759.reading: Make wealth; there is no steel sharper than it for cutting down the pride of enemies.
759.nuance: The target is செருக்கு and not the enemy's body. Parimelazhagar seizes on this: other blades can't cut an intangible. The verse is one of the chapter's few bald imperatives.

760.reading: For those who have made bright wealth in full measure, the other two are easily had, together.
760.nuance: ஒண் does a lot of work: the claim is for bright wealth and not for any wealth. Parimelazhagar reads ஒண் as wealth gained by the right path, while Manakkudavar simply glosses it as bright. Everything else in the claim hinges on that adjective.

links.note: Both make exclusive claims with the same structure. 400 says learning is true wealth and all others are not. 751 says nothing but wealth is anything. The Kural lets each chapter speak in absolutes.

Both use பொய்யா விளக்கு. In 299 the unfailing lamp of the wise is truthfulness and all other lamps are no lamps. Here the same phrase names money. Whether this is a deliberate reversal can't be proved, but the two verses compete for one title.
660 likens wealth made by deceit to water stored in an unfired pot, and Parimelazhagar brings that very image into his comment on 755 to explain why such wealth destroys its maker.
241 ranks grace far above material wealth, which even the base have. 757 makes material wealth the nurse that raises grace. The ranking stands but the independence doesn't.

Two elephant images for getting a task done without personally bearing the risk. In 678 one elephant is used to catch another, and in 758 the owner watches elephants fight. Both separate the one who directs from the danger.

39 says only what flows from virtue is pleasure, so virtue is the source. 760 makes rightly made wealth the ground from which virtue and pleasure both come easily. The order of the three aims differs by book.

source_issues: 752: Parimelazhagar's விளக்கம் repeats his whole word-gloss before the actual comment.
755: Parimelazhagar's word-gloss is missing; only the விளக்கம் is present.
